Week two. Farhan sat with his friend Vijay on the terrace and said, "I keep having the same thoughts." "Then write them down," Vijay said. Farhan didn't.
Week six. On a slow Sunday he took out a notebook and made three headings. What I valued: she listened, and she was funny. What didn't work: we avoided arguments and let things pile up. What I want next time: someone who can talk about small annoyances early, and me, learning to say them. He wrote slowly, sometimes staring at the wall.
Week eight. Vijay asked, "Are you still stuck?" Farhan smiled, a little. "Not stuck. Clearer." He showed Vijay the page.

qa.q: On which week did Farhan take out the notebook?
qa.a: Farhan took out the notebook in week six.

qa.q: What is Farhan feeling at week eight when he shows the page?
qa.a: Farhan feels a quiet clarity and a small smile of relief, saying he is not stuck but clearer.

qa.q: What alternative approach could Farhan add, and why?
qa.a: Farhan could talk it through with a trusted friend as well, because writing sorts thoughts while talking may show a view he cannot see alone.

qa.q: How does Vijay see Farhan's change?
qa.a: Vijay first suggests writing and later asks if Farhan is still stuck, so Vijay watches patiently and is invited to read the page at the end.

grounding: Shows reflecting after some weeks on what was valued, what failed and what is wanted next time, turning pain into clearer ideas about partners.

passage:
Maria, you asked me how I got over my first big breakup. I'm Samir, I'm forty-five, and honestly, I didn't get over it for months. What helped was something my hostel warden made me do.
About six weeks after, I was still moping, and he handed me three sheets of paper. 'Write,' he said. 'What you valued. What didn't work. What you want next time.'
The first page was easy: she made me laugh, she pushed me to read. The second hurt: we never talked about money or family, we just avoided it, and I sulked instead of saying what I felt. The third was short: someone I can argue with kindly, and to be braver about hard talks myself.
I kept those sheets for twenty years. When I met your aunt, I read the third page again.

qa.q: What did the warden hand Samir?
How did Samir feel writing the second page?
qa.a: Samir felt hurt and a bit ashamed, admitting that hard topics were avoided and that sulking replaced saying what was felt.

qa.q: What choice in the story turned the moping into something useful?
qa.a: Accepting the warden's three sheets and writing honestly on each, which turned the pain into clear wishes for next time.

qa.q: How might the warden have seen Samir's moping?
qa.a: The warden likely noticed six weeks of moping and felt it was time for Samir to think, not just feel, so gave a simple task.

grounding: Shows an elder recalling writing what was valued, what failed and what to want next time after a breakup, which gave clearer views for the future.

subtype: Approach: reflecting on what was learned [Thinking]
passage:
It had been seven weeks since Nazia ended things, and Tanvir had an exam in two days. The hostel corridor was loud with a birthday party. He couldn't study, and he couldn't stop thinking about her either.
So he gave himself twenty minutes. He took a page from his rough notebook and made three columns.
What I valued: her patience. How she noticed when I was tired. Our long walks after dinner.
What didn't work: I cancelled plans whenever my cricket team needed me. I never told her when something she said hurt; I went silent for days.
What I want next time: someone who likes walking as much as I do. And me, saying things out loud the same day.
When the twenty minutes ended, the party was still going. But his chest felt looser, and the second column no longer read like a list of her faults. Mostly it was his. He folded the page into his wallet and opened his notes.

qa.q: How long did Tanvir give himself for writing?
How did Tanvir feel when the twenty minutes ended?
qa.a: He felt lighter, his chest looser, and a bit humbled, seeing that the second column was mostly about his own habits.

qa.q: What else could Tanvir do with the page?
qa.a: Reread it after exams, maybe with a friend, and pick one habit, like speaking up the same day, to practise now.

qa.q: How might Nazia see Tanvir's second column if she ever read it?
qa.a: Nazia might feel understood at last, seeing him admit the silences and cancelled plans that hurt her.

grounding: Shows a student writing what was valued, what did not work and what is wanted next time after a breakup, turning pain into clearer views.
